note: County and city data-center actions — moratoriums, permanent ordinances and resolutions — mirrored from the Data Center Community Benefits project's moratoriums.json (snapshot generated 2026-08-04), filtered to city/county/town scope. State-level measures stay in legislation.json; the four instruments that appear in both files are there because legislation.json keeps only the first-of-kind and litigated local measures as full instruments, while this file is the broader table. Records whose action_id starts with 'direct-' were verified directly rather than mirrored. Refresh by fetching docs/data/moratoriums.json from source_repo, mapping each record to this schema, and upserting on action_id — the sync is a pure upsert, never a replace, so nothing here is lost when the upstream snapshot shrinks. Corrections in this file were verified against primary sources on 2026-08-24 and are newer than the mirror: Maine LD 307 was vetoed, not enacted (which is why it is absent here and correct in legislation.json); Hill County TX rescinded its moratorium under a $100M developer suit (superseded, not active); Cleveland's moratorium passed 14-1 on 2026-07-15 (active, not proposed); Indianapolis was finalized 6-0 on 2026-08-19 (active, not proposed); and Monterey Park's Measure NDC passed on 2026-06-02 with 86.4% in favour. A second verification pass (2026-08-24, commit cb9f348) added three more: Cheyenne WY rejected a 12-month (not nine-month) moratorium 8-1 on 2026-05-26, date 2026-05 and source upgraded to WyoFile; Santa Fe County NM voted on 2026-06-30 (not July 1), date 2026-06; Boulder County CO is water_related — the commissioners' announcement cites electricity and water demands. It also stripped the trailing 'Status.' sentence artifact from 13 summaries. Re-apply ALL corrections after any re-sync (the upsert has no field-level protection), and re-check any record still marked 'proposed' whose date is more than about 60 days old. See REFRESH.md.

actions.summary: The Imperial County Board of Supervisors voted 5-0 on June 16, 2026 to adopt an immediate 45-day urgency interim moratorium under California Government Code §65858, pausing approval and permitting of new and pending data center facilities in unincorporated areas; it may be renewed for up to 10 months and 15 days while a 19-member advisory committee develops zoning and building recommendations by January 2027. Residents cited energy and water consumption and environmental/public-health impacts. A developer (Sebastian Rucci) indicated intent to challenge the ordinance in court.

Indio City Council unanimously passed a 45-day emergency data-center moratorium on June 3, 2026, though no data-center proposals were active at the time. The Planning Commission has since recommended an outright ban; the Council is weighing extension versus a permanent ban.

actions.summary: Boulder County commissioners unanimously declared a moratorium of up to 6 months at their June 2, 2026 business meeting, pausing new land-use applications for both data centers and detention facilities in unincorporated Boulder County while staff draft Land Use Code amendments specific to each.

Broomfield joins Longmont, Fort Collins, Boulder, and Larimer County in the Boulder Valley / Northern Colorado wave of pauses.

actions.summary: Denver City Council enacted a 1-year moratorium on May 18, 2026, pausing all new data center facility permits and zoning approvals while the city conducts comprehensive zoning, energy, and water impact assessments. Triggered by: (1) Colorado River Compact water-sharing pressures and acute shortages in the South Platte watershed (Denver's primary source); (2) strains on the Rocky Mountain Power grid during peak summer demand; (3) city's Climate Action Plan goals — Council concerns that unmanaged data center growth could undermine 2040 carbon-neutrality targets. Moratorium covers all facilities, no MW threshold specified. Denver's Office of Energy & Environmental Planning charged with 12-month review of: data center energy consumption projections, renewable energy allocation, water recycling standards, and zoning district revisions. Supported by local environmental groups (Colorado Environmental Law Center, Sierra Club Rocky Mountain Group), labor unions (IBEW Local 68), and water conservation coalitions. Denver International Airport and downtown development interests opposed. Council vote: 11-2 in favor (only two pro-development votes). Industry framed as 'anti-growth'; proponents framed as 'resource stewardship.'

Jefferson County's Board of County Commissioners voted Tuesday, May 19, 2026 to impose a 10-month moratorium on new data center development in the county, running through March 2027 while staff develop land-use regulations specific to the industry.

actions.water_angle: County materials list water consumption among the 'most significant impacts' the pause is meant to study, alongside power usage and siting; a public survey drew 94% opposition to any data-center construction in the county (larimer.gov).
actions.summary: Larimer County's Board of County Commissioners adopted a resolution on January 27, 2026 pausing new land-use applications for data center facilities in unincorporated Larimer County, then extended it on February 9, 2026 through August 25, 2026 to give staff time to draft permanent regulations; a public survey drew 94% opposition to any data center construction in the county.

actions.water_angle: Town board members and roughly 20 residents cited Colorado's active drought and one of its warmest, driest winters on record as the water-scarcity rationale for a pre-emptive pause; no developer had yet approached the town.
actions.summary: Lochbuie's Town Board voted 6-1 on July 21, 2026 to pass a five-year moratorium on data-center facility applications — the longest active data-center pause in Colorado. Proactive measure (Mayor Jamie Jeffery said no developer had approached the town), passed amid statewide drought conditions. Found via an Aug. 10, 2026 Colorado moratorium roundup (KUNC/Colorado Newsline), not present in the DCCB moratoriums.json mirror.

actions.summary: Longmont City Council passed Ordinance 2026-34 on a 6-1 vote June 9, 2026: data centers with 100 MW or more of projected or contracted peak demand (at opening or through phased expansion) are permanently banned as a land use, while smaller facilities in Primary Employment zones remain permitted subject to new energy-efficiency, water, cooling, noise, and lighting standards.

Monument's town council voted Monday, July 20, 2026 to place a proactive 6-month ban on new data center applications — no project has yet been proposed in town, but officials wanted rules in place before one arrives. Monument is the first municipality in El Paso County to adopt a data center moratorium, following Woodland Park's ordinance days earlier.

Woodland Park City Council passed an ordinance at its July 16, 2026 meeting imposing an 18-month moratorium on the submission, acceptance, processing, and approval of data center applications, giving the city time to study county-level rules and draft its own zoning use standards.

Two secondary sources (a July 1 opinion column and a July 27 op-ed) describe the moratorium as already adopted, but neither is a neutral news report confirming the vote, so status is left as proposed pending a cleaner source. Triggered by resident concerns about data center energy and water impacts. Part of the broader wave of Central/North Florida county moratoriums under the 1-year pathway created by Florida SB484.

actions.summary: Jackson County (Florida Panhandle) Board of Commissioners enacted a permanent ban on new data centers in unincorporated portions of the county on June 15, 2026. The action began as a temporary moratorium, but commissioners voted to amend the ordinance into a permanent prohibition — making it one of the strongest data center restrictions in Florida. Jackson County's permanent ban appears to conflict with Florida SB484 (signed May 7, 2026), which restricts local governments from permanently banning data centers. The legal status of the ban may be subject to challenge.

actions.water_angle: Led by Commissioner Anthony Sabatini, who cited 12 data center applications filed in Florida in the past year and concerns about water usage and electricity grid impacts.
actions.summary: Lake County (central Florida) commissioners proposed a 12-month moratorium on new data center development on June 24, 2026, with a final adoption vote scheduled within two weeks. Led by Commissioner Anthony Sabatini, who cited 12 data center applications filed in Florida in the past year and concerns about water usage and electricity grid impacts. Sabatini framed the moratorium as necessary because Florida's SB484 (signed May 7) restricts outright permanent bans, leaving moratoria of up to one year as the available tool. Status re-check 2026-07-26: the commission unanimously agreed to pursue an ordinance, but no ordinance has been drafted and no adoption vote has been scheduled. This is a direction to staff, not yet a moratorium.

actions.water_angle: Following resident concerns about energy and water impacts.
actions.summary: Pasco County (west-central Florida) commissioners passed the first reading of a one-year moratorium on large-scale data center development on June 12, 2026, then adopted it on final vote July 14, 2026, with a 2.5 MW threshold (reduced from an originally proposed 10 MW). Following resident concerns about energy and water impacts. Part of a broader wave of Central/North Florida county moratoriums enacted in mid-2026. Florida's SB484 (signed May 7) restricts permanent bans but allows moratoria of up to one year, which is why multiple Florida counties moved in concert.

Sarasota County (southwest Florida) commissioners voted 5-0 on July 9, 2026 to stop accepting or reviewing data center applications for one year, after the county was approached by a company interested in a Cattleman Road property. No formal applications had been received; the pause gives staff time to evaluate how data centers fit the zoning code before any are considered. Part of the broader wave of Florida county moratoriums enacted under the 1-year pathway created by Florida SB484.

On July 6, 2026 the Taylor County (Florida) Commission declined to adopt a proposed data center moratorium — recommended by Commissioner Pam Feagle to run through December 31 — with the motion failing for lack of support after Commissioner Michael Newman said he lacked sufficient information to back the policy. Commissioners agreed to hold a data center workshop on August 25, 2026.

Commissioners then voted unanimously around April 7-8, 2026 to lift the moratorium and replace it with permanent regulations restricting new data centers to heavy-industrial zoning and requiring closed-loop cooling.

Asbury City Council unanimously approved a 180-day data-center freeze, effective immediately, to evaluate the impacts of data centers on land, infrastructure, and the environment.

The Boone County Board of Commissioners unanimously enacted a one-year moratorium pausing the filing, processing, review, and acceptance of applications for new data center facilities in unincorporated areas, effective June 16, 2026 through June 15, 2027. Officials noted neither the 2009 Comprehensive Plan nor the 1998 Zoning Ordinance contemplated modern data center development and its impacts on land use, infrastructure, utilities, agriculture, and rural character.
Indianapolis-Marion County Council passed non-binding resolution expressing opposition to large, unrestricted data center development without community input and environmental safeguards.

actions.water_angle: Adopted on condition that the city study water and electricity impacts, alongside campus size and noise, before new applications resume.
actions.summary: A binding data-center moratorium — distinct from the non-binding 2024 council resolution — advanced 10-3 out of the Metropolitan & Economic Development Committee on July 13, 2026, passed the City-County Council 23-1 on August 10, and was finalized 6-0 by the Metropolitan Development Commission on August 19. It bars new data-center approvals in Marion County through December 31, 2027, exempting three already-approved projects (DC Blox, Metrobloks, Sabey). A companion special-use zoning class (SU-47) for data centers is advancing alongside it.

Marshall County commissioners voted on April 20, 2026 to permanently ban data centers countywide — described as the first permanent data center ban in Indiana, not a temporary moratorium. Commissioners cited unresolved safety and environmental concerns, including the risk of a hazardous-materials ('HAZMAT') site; companion restrictions on solar and battery storage were advanced the same session. Enacted (permanent ban).

New Albany, Indiana (across the Ohio River from Louisville, KY) City Council unanimously enacted a one-year moratorium on new data center development at its July 16, 2026 meeting, following Mayor Jeff Gahan's June 9 call for a pause and a Plan Commission recommendation. The ordinance blocks new data centers — single buildings or multi-building campuses — exceeding 100,000 sq ft while the city studies impacts on infrastructure, utilities, environment, and noise and updates its zoning ordinance. City leaders cited the $800M Meta data center under construction in neighboring Jeffersonville as an example of the scale the city wants to plan ahead of.

actions.summary: The Harvey County Commission unanimously enacted a moratorium on January 13, 2026 halting construction of data centers in unincorporated Harvey County through 2028, to give planning, zoning and environmental staff time to develop regulations; the commission may rescind or extend it at any time. Officials cited power and water concerns raised by nearby communities (Andale, Colwich). No data center application had been filed at the time.

actions.summary: Cave City (Barren County, KY) council enacted a 12-month moratorium on data center construction and expansion on May 21, 2026, by a 4-1 vote. Councilmember Denny Doyle cast the lone dissenting vote. Motivated by community concerns about a proposed large-scale data center and its impacts on local resources. Following enactment, Kentucky Industrial Alliance LLC filed a lawsuit against the City of Cave City, the city council, and the Barren County planning commission — making Cave City's moratorium one of the first in the country to face legal challenge from a developer.

Lexington-Fayette Urban County Council unanimously passed a moratorium on new data center approvals on June 9, 2026, pausing all permits, development plan acceptances, and zone changes related to data centers until October 31, 2026. Triggered by DartPoints Operating Company's $29M acquisition of the former Lexmark data center on New Circle Road, with plans to expand to 20–70 MW. Mayor Linda Gorton backed the measure, citing concerns that data centers 'do not produce many jobs and have the potential to increase utility costs on local residents.' The council simultaneously launched a Zoning Ordinance Text Amendment process to develop modern data center regulations, with a Planning Commission public hearing expected in late July and Council recommendations in August.

On January 28, 2026 the New Orleans City Council adopted Motion M-26-63 (with companion study motion M-26-62), directing the City Planning Commission to create a temporary Data Center Interim Zoning District that pauses occupational licenses and approvals for data centers, server farms and cryptocurrency-mining facilities citywide for one year. It followed a proposed AI data center in New Orleans East.

A Greenfield city councilor is proposing a one-year data-center moratorium as an ordinance (rather than a slower zoning amendment). No data centers have been proposed in Greenfield yet — a proactive measure, not a response to a pending project.

actions.summary: Baltimore enacted a moratorium on data centers exceeding 10 MW (May 2026) due to concerns about grid strain on aging infrastructure, water demands during drought, and lack of community input. Supported by environmental groups and residents. Reflects growing municipal scrutiny of data center siting without environmental review. Baltimore explores requirements for energy audits, water conservation plans, and community benefit agreements. City working with utilities to assess grid capacity constraints.

actions.summary: The Montgomery County Council voted 11-0 on July 28, 2026 to adopt an 18-month moratorium (Expedited Bill 19-26) barring the Department of Permitting Services from issuing new data center permits, alongside a companion Zoning Text Amendment (ZTA 26-01) establishing a data-center definition and limitations in the zoning code. Cited concerns: Potomac River protection, ratepayer/electric-bill impact, noise, water use, and the absence of an existing zoning definition for data centers; a state-level study is due to the Governor and General Assembly by September 1, 2026. The 18-month term was a compromise between an initial 6-month proposal (Councilmember Evan Glass) and a 2-year proposal (Councilmembers Will Jawando and Kristin Mink), and follows an interim 6-month moratorium County Executive Marc Elrich had already imposed by executive order in June 2026. Existing, already-operating data centers are exempt. Atmosphere's proposed Dickerson data center (a former coal-plant site) is among the affected pending proposals.

actions.summary: The Prince George's County Council approved a resolution on July 7, 2026 establishing a moratorium of up to two years on new hyperscale data center development, barring the planning department from considering or approving applications until the Council enacts regulatory legislation (or adopts a zoning framework). Council members cited unanswered questions about water, health, environmental, and utility impacts. Council Member Tim Adams voted against and three members abstained.

actions.summary: The Washington County (Maryland) Board of County Commissioners voted 4-1 on June 30, 2026 to adopt a one-year moratorium on data center applications and development, to study impacts on utility infrastructure, water, noise, and environmental risks. Commissioners Wagner, Leatherman, Cline, and Barr voted yes; Commissioner Neil Parrott opposed. Concerns cited: high energy consumption straining utilities, noise from cooling systems and backup generators, substantial water use, hazardous materials and e-waste, and rural/agricultural land-use compatibility.

Cleveland City Council approved a three-month moratorium on new standalone data-center construction and expansions by a 14-1 vote on July 15, 2026, after shortening an original one-year proposal. Applies only to standalone data-center buildings, not server rooms in multi-tenant or mixed-use properties; gives City Hall time to craft zoning rules, with council able to extend past the three months.

On April 21, 2026 the Oklahoma City Council unanimously approved an emergency moratorium halting new applications and rezoning/permits for data-center construction or expansion through December 31, 2026, while staff evaluate concerns and possible code changes. Two pending rezoning cases are exempt; a May 2026 amendment allowed data centers up to 75 MW to apply.

Chesterfield County Council (South Carolina) unanimously passed a data center moratorium running through January 1, 2028, after a unanimous first reading in April 2026 and unanimous second reading in early May 2026. Proposed by Code Enforcement Director Derrick Outten and Councilman Donald Kirkley. The county had no prior ordinance or code definition for data centers. Cited concerns: high electricity consumption raising residential rates, noise complaints, and limited job creation relative to facility size. No data centers currently operate in the county. Sourcing note: the Progressive Journal (primary source) places the unanimous second reading in early May 2026; a later Go Laurens roundup describes the Chesterfield ordinance as enacted in early June 2026. The May date from the primary source is used here; the discrepancy is unresolved and the enacted_date should be re-checked against the county council minutes.

actions.summary: Colleton County Council (South Carolina) unanimously approved first reading on May 4, 2026 of an ordinance imposing a 6-month moratorium on special exceptions, conditional-use approvals, and other land-use/development approvals for data centers, giving officials time to revise the land-use code. Follows a proposed ~1 GW data center (Thomas & Hutton / Eagle Rock Partners) on 850 acres of Weyerhaeuser timberland near the environmentally sensitive ACE Basin, south of Walterboro, that drew opposition from seven state legislators and hundreds of residents at a public hearing. Two more readings are required under South Carolina's three-reading ordinance process; no second-reading date set as of this record.

Greenwood County Council (South Carolina) introduced Ordinance 2026-25 on first reading June 19, 2026, proposing a 12-month moratorium on new data center and related-infrastructure approvals so the county can study zoning, noise, setback, heat, and energy-demand standards. Sponsored by Councilmembers Mark Allison and Cathy Miller and Vice Chairman Dayne Pruitt. Second reading and public hearing set for July 7, 2026. The county Planning Commission had separately recommended denying a related data center text amendment (Ordinance 2026-19) and suggested a longer 24-month pause.

Residents packed a public hearing at the county opera house citing water-supply strain, electric-rate increases, and continuous industrial noise.

actions.summary: Spartanburg County Council (South Carolina) approved the first reading of a 12-month data center moratorium on June 22, 2026, with no dissenting votes. Two additional readings are required before full enactment. Council immediately invoked the pending ordinance doctrine, allowing the county to halt new data center permit applications after first reading — the protective effect begins at first reading even before final passage. Triggered by a company filing a land development permit for a data center at 300 Jones Road without local tax incentives. A separate state bill (SC H.5526) proposing a statewide data center moratorium is also before the legislature.

actions.water_angle: County will weigh water supply as one siting factor (with proximity to sensitive land uses, road access, and environmental impact) when defining where energy-development zones may locate; not cited as the moratorium's primary driver.
actions.summary: Austin County commissioners unanimously enacted a countywide moratorium on new AI data centers and battery energy storage systems on July 28, 2026, following a July 13 public hearing that drew 100+ residents. Not an outright ban — gives the county time to evaluate impacts before defining where such facilities may locate. Found via the Part 1 sweep (MultiState, 2026-08-19), not present in the DCCB moratoriums.json mirror.

actions.summary: Fort Worth City Council voted unanimously on Aug. 11, 2026 to take first steps toward a 90-day data-center construction moratorium: created the Fort Worth Data Center & Infrastructure Commission (a review panel with community representatives) and adopted an ordinance requiring new data-center applications to show PUC/ERCOT grid-interconnection approval. The moratorium itself needs further public hearings before formal adoption; it would exempt projects already in the pipeline and, if adopted, would take effect in 2027.
Hill County enacted moratorium on new data center facilities. Moratorium is currently under legal challenge by development interests.

Council Bill 121214 passed unanimously (9-0) on June 9, 2026, placing a temporary freeze on new data-center siting (facilities with power capacity over 20 megavolt-amperes). Took effect immediately under its emergency designation. Companion Resolution 32204 establishes a policy-study framework; a public hearing is required within 60 days.

actions.summary: The Oneida County (Wisconsin) Planning and Development Committee unanimously passed an interim data center moratorium ordinance amendment that would bar the county from accepting, processing, or approving new data center developments for at least one year while it develops regulations. It still requires full County Board approval, expected on the August 2026 agenda; it excludes un-zoned towns and the City of Rhinelander. Concerns cited: water and electricity consumption, noise, and potential pollution.

City council rejected a proposed 12-month moratorium on data center facility permits 8-1 on May 26, 2026; sponsor Mark Moody cast the lone yes vote. The proposal would have paused permits pending an infrastructure assessment.
